initial_observation.encounter_context: admitted to our hospital because of an episode of seizures and transient left hemiparesis
initial_observation.chief_complaint: episode of seizures and transient left hemiparesis
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: clinical history significant for repeated episodes of epistaxis and for exertional dyspnea; clinical examination remarkable for pale skin and cyanosis of the nails; small cutaneous telangiectases on the face initially considered not significant; oxygen saturation 82% on ambient air; severe iron deficiency anemia
presenting_symptoms: small cutaneous telangiectases on the face

evidence_items.source_text: laboratory exams showed severe iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin level 5.8 g/dl, normal values 12 to 16; serum ferritin level 4 ng/ml, normal range 11 to 307). Fecal occult blood was positive.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed increased signal intensity on diffusion weighted imaging in the cerebellum without associated contrast enhancement, as for ischemic stroke.
Gastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal, while a capsule endoscopy documented multiple telangiectasias in the jejunum, and oral iron supplements were started after a blood trasfusion.

To investigate the hypoxia a chest and abdomen computed tomography (CT) with administration of intravenous contrast material was ordered. The exam showed a group of dilated vessels in right upper and lower pulmonary lobes. These lesions were reported as likely arteriovenous malformations (PAVM) (Figure 1 and 2). The CT of the abdomen was unremarkable.

Right heart catheterization was performed and a 8 french catheter was introduced first in the right lower lobar pulmonary artery and then in the upper one. The angiography confirmed the PAVMs and the feeding arteries were embolized through coil occlusion. The procedure led to the exclusion of the PAVMs from the pulmonary circulation (Figure 3 and 4).
The association of recurrent nasal bleeds, cutaneous telangiectasias and visceral vascular malformations allowed us to diagnose HHT (see below).
